newsitem.title: USA: Insurance settlements expanding from AIDS origins.
newsitem.headline: Insurance settlements expanding from AIDS origins.

text.p: Several years into a 10-year fight with cancer, 39-year-old Lawrence Imbordino was told his condition was terminal.

The illness has been tough on the jazz musician's family as well. Though he had medical insurance, Imbordino was faced with thousands of dollars of out-of-pocket medical costs that almost forced him to sell his house in a hurry.
But last year, he opted to sell his life insurance policy for less than its face value so he would have money to meet his bills and do something special for his wife and children.
"I did a little of both," Imbordino said of his decision to use his $30,000 settlement to take his family to Disney World and to pay some bills. "I took care of myself and my bill collectors.
"The settlement helped us get our head above water, a little bit," he said.
Imbordino may represent a trend in the so-called viatical settlement industry, which started by paying off settlements for AIDS patients in the early part of the decade.

With greater acceptance of the settlements and news of promising treatments for AIDS, some in the industry expect cancer patients to overtake AIDS patients as the primary recipients of viatical settlements.
One company planning on that transition is Viaticus Inc., a unit of CNA Financial Corp., and a major player in the industry.

"Certainly, Viaticus would expect that cancer would become the leading condition that we help by the end of next year," Viaticus President Gary Chodes said in a recent interview. "Other companies probably aren't going to make the transition in the same way.
"Within AIDS, that market is becoming more mature and with some of the treatment protocols that come out, it makes some of the people with AIDS not eligible for viatical settlement," Chodes said.

Dignity Partners Inc. said in July that it was temporarily ceasing to process new applications from individuals diagnosed with AIDS and the virus that causes it while it further analyses research results on AIDS treatments presented at the International AIDS conference this summer. Last week, the San Francisco-based company said that analysis was continuing.
A provision in recently passed healthcare legislation would allow payments to patients expected to die within two years to be tax exempt.

Chodes said he expected this to help expand use of viatical settlements for people other than AIDS patients. He noted that cancer accounts for a far greater percentage of deaths in the United States than AIDS.
"There isn't any particular reason why a cancer patient wouldn't be as good if not better candidate" for a settlement, he said.
Viaticus estimated that about $800 million in policies will be purchased by the industry in viatical settlements this year, with the figure jumping to over $1 billion by 1998.
"That rate is going to rapidly increase," he said, adding that Viaticus, which buys nearly a third of the $500 million in policies it considers, will grow with that business.
While 50 percent of Viaticus' business currently comes from AIDS patients, Chodes expects that to drop to 25 percent next year.

Viaticus pays up to 85 percent of the face value of a policy to a terminally ill person, maintains the premium on the policy, and then collects the full value when the person dies. Its decision whether to accept a policy and how much to pay is based on premium cost, life expectancy and terms of the policy.
While receiving the settlement was helpful, it was also stressful, Imbordino said.
"To be approved for it also says that everybody agrees that 'Yeah, you're in pretty big trouble, pal,'" he said.
Imbordino said he received about 75 percent of the value of his policy, which helped postpone a decision to sell his house for more than a year.
The house is now on the market and he has sold one of the family's two cars, but the settlement gave him some time to plan.
"This would have happened maybe much more catastrophically if we weren't able to get the benefit from Viaticus," Imbordino said.
